1:
The superscription is where the commentators settle the book's authorship, and they do not agree. Delitzsch reports that the ancients, having this line in view, regarded the whole as Solomon's, and that the gap between the book's length and the three thousand proverbs credited to him was met by the rabbinic suggestion that each verse divides in two. Henry holds these to be of Solomon's own writing and divinely inspired, distinguishing them from the three thousand his servants collected into day-books, and adds the tradition that the apocryphal books of wisdom were compiled out of the uninspired remainder. Clarke states the contrary plainly: he thinks it very likely Solomon did not compose them all, but gathered everything of the kind within reach and condensed what agreed with the Spirit of truth. He answers the charge that this derogates from the book's authority by arguing that whatever truth is found among men came originally from God, who may claim his own wherever it is found and give it a new authentication.

The counting is done twice and does not tally. Gill reckons six hundred and fifty-nine verses apart from the first nine chapters, which he treats as introduction, and nine hundred and fifteen with them, not a third of the three thousand. Delitzsch gives the figure as eight hundred. Neither reconciles his count with the other, and Gill's conclusion is simply that here are as many and such as God thought fit should be preserved.

On what a proverb is, the two etymologies pull apart. Clarke derives the Latin from a word standing in place of a whole discourse, illustrating it with a rabbinic saying in which lamp means both revelation and the human soul; but the Hebrew, he notes, comes from a root meaning to rule, so that the word signifies weighty and therefore authoritative sayings by which a man's whole conduct is governed. Gill finds both senses in the one root, similitude and dominion together, and notes the custom of the ancients everywhere of wrapping a truth established by experience in a few apt words so that it might be better retained, these differing only in being inspired. Ellicott refers the reader to his introduction for the range of the Hebrew word.

Two of them explain the book by the reign that produced it, and in almost the same words. Henry sets Solomon beside his father: David, whose life was full of troubles, wrote a book of devotion, and Solomon, who lived quietly, a book of instruction, since when the churches had rest they were edified. Ellicott makes the same contrast, the quiet and prosperity of the peaceful king's reign favouring a sententious philosophy where his father's wars and danger had called forth impassioned eloquence. Henry presses the name itself, which signifies peaceable, and observes that it was no disparagement to a king to be an instructor of the ignorant.

Clarke's introduction then runs well past the verse. He traces proverbial wisdom outward from the first worshippers of God to the heathen who dealt with them, so that no ancient nation lacks such a code, and names the Sanscrit, Persian and Arabic collections and the fable-books of antiquity. Yet he also argues from chronology that Solomon reigned centuries before every famous Gentile moralist, and concludes that to the Gentiles he could be little if at all indebted, which sits awkwardly beside his own opening concession. He divides the book into five parts, notes that the Greek version takes greater liberty with this text than any other and is the one quoted in the New Testament, regrets that Solomon's natural history of trees, beasts, fowls and fishes is wholly lost, and describes the illuminated vellum folio on his own shelf, older in its language than Wiclif, which once belonged to a son of Edward the Third.
2:
These verses are the book's own statement of purpose, read as a chain rather than a list. Delitzsch shows the structure: the first half of the opening aim is expanded through the next three verses and the second half in the last, the whole being one sustained infinitive construction. Ellicott says the writer heaps up synonyms to bring out how wide the purpose is. Gill takes the range as broad as it goes, calling the book Solomon's ethics, his politics since it instructs kings and subjects, and his economics since it gives rules for husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and servants; its final business, he adds, is the knowledge of Christ, who is the wisdom of God.

The two governing words are pressed hard. Delitzsch traces the first to a root meaning to be firm or closed, so that it denotes compactness and then ability and prudence, noting that an earlier scholar had already fixed the sense as solidity. Ellicott renders the same root as firmness, an opinion resting on sound reasons, set against the mind carried about with every wind of doctrine. On the second word he departs from the English: better discipline, the knowledge of how to keep oneself under control. Clarke widens it instead, taking the first word for the whole heavenly teaching that shows us both ourselves and God, and the second for the teaching that discovers all its parts. Wesley divides it briefly into human wisdom for the conduct of affairs and divine wisdom, the instruction coming either from God or from men.

The word for the simple produces the section's longest note, and it is Clarke's. He traces the English through its Latin parts, without a fold, then follows its decay from unmixed to innocent to homely and at last to silly, a degradation he blames on the rarity of plain dealing. He distinguishes two Hebrew words usually derived from one root, one from a verb meaning to be rash and the other from a verb meaning to entice, the first being used here. Ellicott defines it as those open to good impressions who are also easily led astray. Delitzsch is more technical, noting the plural written here in a mongrel form combining two spellings, and explaining the root as to be open, so that the word means one whose heart stands open to every influence, a term that could go either way but usually goes the worse.

The subtlety promised such men is felt as a difficulty. Gill answers by appeal to the serpent and the dove, so that the simple may become wise as serpents while remaining harmless, and wary of being drawn aside by the old serpent. Ellicott makes the same move, noting that the Hebrew word is elsewhere used for guile, and gathering the sayings about the wisdom of serpents and the shrewdness of the children of this world.

The last two verses turn to those who are already wise. Delitzsch notes that the infinitives here pass into independent sentences for variety, and that the verb is jussive rather than future, an invitation and not a prediction. Clarke hears the same widening of the audience and sets beside it an old English rendering, that by hearing the wise man shall come by more wisdom. Ellicott gives the phrase for wise counsels its literal sense, arts of seamanship, steering oneself and others through rough water; Wesley calls it plainly the art of governing himself or others. On the closing pair Gill takes the second word for the elegance of the saying and Ellicott for an obscure thing needing interpretation, while Delitzsch derives it from a root meaning twisted, speech turned aside rather than open, connecting it with the word for a mocker as one who uses oblique words. The dark sayings Ellicott calls literally knots; Clarke thinks the Gospel parables come nearest to what is meant.
7:
Here the book proper begins, and they all say so. Delitzsch calls the verse the motto and device of the whole, and notes that the Hebrew for beginning carries both senses at once, the point one starts from and the basis one stands on, root as well as opening. Gill says plainly that this is the first of the proverbs and that nothing like it is found in all the writings of the heathen. Ellicott counts the phrase thirteen times in the book and treats the distich as the key-note to all that follows. Henry unpacks the claim three ways: of all things to be known this is most evident, so those ignorant of it know nothing; a mind without holy reverence cannot profit by instruction; and all knowledge must tend back to the fear of God as its centre, both alpha and omega.

What the fear itself is gets defined carefully and differently. Gill rules out a servile fear of punishment and insists on a filial fear presupposing knowledge of God as a father and of his forgiving love, which takes in the whole of religious worship. Clarke defines it as the reverence every intelligent being owes his Creator, then asks what religion is and answers with the two commandments, since without love there is no obedience and without reverence no perseverance. Wesley compresses it to reverence and obedience. Ellicott alone treats the phrase historically and as superseded: the law was enforced by threat because men had to be taught how hateful sin is, but the new covenant preached a new motive, so that the fear of the Lord may be the beginning of wisdom while something better is still to be aimed at, since he that feareth is not made perfect in love.

On the fools who despise it the definitions again diverge. Henry takes them for atheists who set God at defiance and so have no desire to know his ways. Clarke renders the Hebrew simply as evil men, of bad hearts, heads and ways; Ellicott makes them self-willed persons who will listen to no advice; Wesley calls them wicked men so far from attaining wisdom that they despise the means of getting it.

The turn to the parents is read as deliberate sequence. Gill observes that Solomon proceeds in the order of the ten commandments, the first table concerning God's worship and the second opening with the honour due to father and mother. Henry notices the same pattern in a pagan source, where a Greek philosopher's golden verses open with the same two rules, the first in a wretchedly corrupted state. He adds that where Gentile ethics and the laws of Persia and Rome secured only the father's honour, the divine law secures the mother's also. Delitzsch and Clarke both note that father and son were the titles of teacher and pupil, Delitzsch adding that the Talmud's reading of the father as God and the mother as the nation is practical application, not grammatical sense. Clarke insists on the literal household: the father is often abroad earning the family's support and instructs occasionally, while the mother is constantly indoors and so regulates the house and gives laws.

The ornament is taken two ways. Gill and Delitzsch both make it the fairest adornment a child can wear, Delitzsch rendering the phrase a graceful crown, from a root meaning to wind. Henry raises it to a badge of first-rate honour, worth more in God's sight than a gold chain, and says those are truly valuable who value themselves by their piety rather than their wealth. Clarke follows the metaphor into a maxim: since a chain about the neck has marked political dignity in many nations, the surest way to eminence in civil affairs is to act on the principles of wisdom. Ellicott names Joseph and Daniel, rewarded with exactly that.
10:
The enticement is the third of the opening rules, after the fear of God and the honour of parents. Henry notes that the psalms open with the same caution, that the seducers do not threaten or argue but flatter, and that they mistake if they think sharing their guilt lessens their reckoning, since it only increases what they must answer for. Gill is careful about who is meant: not sinners by infirmity, but notorious offenders whose trade is sin, hardened enough to want company in it. Delitzsch reads the Hebrew intensive the same way, as men in whom sin has become habit, and derives the verb for entice from a root meaning to open, so that it is to make a man accessible to persuasion. Clarke makes the answering verb the hinge of the passage: they can do no harm unless the will joins them, and God's purpose is that the will never be forced, since otherwise he could not judge the world.

Whether the scene is literal divides them. Ellicott takes it as a warning against brigandage, a crime to which the country was always exposed by its broken terrain and predatory neighbours. Clarke agrees that the words are exactly what is spoken when a gang of cutthroats forms, and glosses the invitation to cast in a lot as being made a sworn brother with an equal share. Henry treats the highwaymen as a specimen only, standing for every evil into which sinners entice men, and traces the courtship as it rises, from come with us at first to a shared purse at last.

On the swallowing alive, Delitzsch says the phrase alludes in fact and wording to the fate of Korah's company, and Ellicott names the same episode; Gill keeps it practical, the gang large enough to bury the victims so that no witness remains. Clarke enlarges the scene to a whole village destroyed, so the property may be carried off. Henry turns their precious substance against them: it is neither substance nor precious, and those who trade with sin promise themselves mighty bargains but only dream that they eat, the houseful dwindling to a handful.

The reasons against joining them are counted out. Ellicott numbers two, the horrible nature of the crime and their folly, since the net they hid will take their own foot. Delitzsch counts three, the immorality of the conduct, the audaciousness of the seduction and the self-destruction, the third introduced by a simple connective after two causal ones. On the bird and the net the readings diverge. Gill offers two, that the innocent are caught without cause as a bird is, or that the bird is so intent on the corn that it misses the net; Clarke and Delitzsch take the proverb straightforwardly, that a net spread in sight is spread in vain, Delitzsch dismissing the reading that makes it a net strewn with bait. Henry and Wesley press the comparison further than the proverb does: these men are worse than birds, for the fowler at least knows to conceal his snare, while the sinner sees the jail and the gallows at the end of his road and rushes on regardless.

The close is agreed and sharpened by Clarke. Gill, Wesley and Ellicott read the ambush as recoiling on the men who set it, Ellicott adding that God will deliver the innocent and bring the mischief on their own heads. Delitzsch makes covetousness itself the subject that takes away the life, and notes the idiom by which a man is called the owner of the vice he holds; Ellicott gives the same idiom its parallels, the owner of anger and of appetite. Clarke turns the verse on his own readers: a covetous man is in God's sight a murderer, and he instances the tradesman who opens shop after shop in one neighbourhood and undersells his rivals, careless how many families starve.
20:
Who Wisdom is here is the chapter's largest question, and the answers form a spectrum. Gill rules out the alternatives one by one: not the divine attribute displayed in creation, not the light of nature, not the law of Moses, not revelation in general nor the Gospel in particular, but Christ, since what is ascribed to Wisdom in this book belongs properly to a divine person. Clarke stands at the other end: the personification means nothing beyond the teaching given to man by revelation or by the Spirit's voice in the heart, of which common sense and the law written on the heart are instances. Wesley takes it as the wisdom of God revealed in his word, crying loudly to show his earnestness. Henry keeps every stage of the range: human understanding is wisdom, and conscience is God's voice and not always a still small one; civil government is wisdom, magistrates being his vicegerents; revelation is wisdom; and Christ himself is Wisdom, so that it is he who both pleads and passes sentence here.

Ellicott alone shows his working. He takes the form as a plural meaning the manifold excellences of wisdom, and allows that Solomon may have meant no more than a poetic description of those in whom the fear of the Lord dwells. He then argues for the higher reading by analogy with the psalms, which describe an earthly king yet find completion elsewhere, and by evidence: a saying attributed to the wisdom of God in one gospel is spoken by Christ in his own person in another, so that from the earliest Christian times the passage has been held prophetic, and there is good reason for the view.

That the crying is public matters to all. Delitzsch counts it precisely, four times that Wisdom goes forth preaching and four that she preaches publicly, and notes that the repeated word for the city implies she preaches not in the field before a few but where the people are crowded. He explains the phrase for the chief place as the point from which streets divide, comparing the Arabic idioms for the head of a spring and of a river. Henry gathers the parallels: it is comfortable to cast the gospel net where the fish are many, Christ taught openly and in secret said nothing, and truth seeks no corners. Wesley notes the gates as the place of judgment and adds that the cry is not in the gate only but throughout the city. Ellicott gives the crying a different force: she cannot bear to see sinners rushing on their doom.

The three classes addressed are sorted alike by everyone and characterized differently. Delitzsch defines them from their roots: the simple as those accessible to seduction, the scorners as free-thinkers, from a root meaning to twist, men who use oblique words, and the fools as the mentally coarse and indolent. He notes a small point of tense with a large sense: the verbs of loving and hating stand in the future for what continues, while the verb for the scorners' pleasure stands in the perfect, naming what they had already made their object; and Wisdom addresses only the simple by name, expecting to reach them soonest. Ellicott adds that the name for the scorners first appears in Solomon's time, when prosperity favoured religious indifference and scepticism, and that a prophet had to deal with the same men later. Henry is harshest, calling the scorners the worst of sinners and the fools who hate knowledge the worst of fools; but he softens it by noting that the question how long implies God desires their conversion and not their ruin, and waits to be gracious. Gill turns the address on the Jews of the gospels, the simple being those first called by Christ and despised as unlearned; Clarke says only that these are men who have been seduced.
23:
The offer comes first, and is read as conditional. Delitzsch argues the grammar: the clause is not a wish, which would need a particle the text lacks, and the following behold marks the first half as the condition, so that if they would turn, the Spirit would be poured out. Gill agrees for another reason: this is not a call to conversion of the heart, which is God's work, but to turning the face and ears toward the preached word. Clarke translates it as at my convincing mode of arguing, which he claims is properly the sense of the original. Ellicott hears in the outpouring the prophecy fulfilled at Pentecost; Wesley reads the next clause as the Spirit making the word understood.

Then the pause. Delitzsch marks it between the two verses: Wisdom, having waited in vain, turns her call to repentance into a discourse announcing judgment. Ellicott puts it as a change of tone from mercy to judgment. Gill distinguishes the internal call by special grace, effectual and never refused, from the external call by the word, which often is. Wesley widens the calling to ministers, judgments, and the motions of Spirit and conscience alike.

Clarke then breaks with all of them on what is being threatened. He takes the passage as spoken of the robbers described earlier, now caught and about to suffer what the law demands, wishing too late they had chosen the fear of the Lord. Nothing here, he states flatly, applies to their eternal state, much less to any man convinced of sin: men condemned to die may call on justice earnestly and call in vain, but no penitent this side of eternity seeks pardon through Christ without being heard, since life is the time of probation and only in eternity is the state fixed. Gill reads the same verses of the Jews and their destruction by Rome. Ellicott keeps the parable's door, shut at last because they would not call while he was near.

The laughter is felt as a difficulty. Gill calls it an anthropopathy and reads it as retaliation, measure for measure: no mercy will be shown, and God will take pleasure in the glory of his justice. Ellicott will not go so far: such expressions are not literal, since human folly can give God no pleasure, and they mean only that he will act as if he mocked when he refuses to hear. Delitzsch derives the word for calamity from a root meaning to oppress, and observes that the terror named is not what these men dread, since they are secure, but what will frighten them when it comes. Clarke notes of the whirlwind that sense and sound are well matched in the Hebrew.

The last verses divide sharply. Delitzsch takes the noun for turning in its second sense, desertion rather than conversion, so apostasy from wisdom and from God are joined in one word, and reads the next term as carnal security while allowing it can elsewhere mean the peace of the righteous. Ellicott and Wesley agree the turning is away from God, Ellicott glossing the prosperity as the apathy of dull people who cannot believe God will fulfil his threats. Gill offers the aversion of the Jews to Christ, and reports another reading making it the rest of the simple, who take their ease in ceremonies and cry peace when destruction is at hand. Clarke alone leaves the register, taking it as turning king's evidence, an accomplice saving his life by impeaching his gang, likeliest to turn because he was one of the seduced, and giving that evidence while the others were secure in their spoil. On the closing promise they converge, Clarke rendering it that the man shall inhabit safety itself, quiet from fear because conscious of his innocence and of God's protection, and setting against it the tag that what is ill gotten is worse spent.
